name: Homelab Detection Coverage
description: 12 techniques covered across dc-01/rtr-01 (Linux/AD, mostly custom rules against sparse default Samba logging) and ws-01 (Windows/Sysmon, mostly verifying Wazuh's mature stock ruleset), plus SCA remediation and one honestly-documented gap. See phase-4-detection/detection-catalog.md for full methodology, verification evidence, and evasion notes per technique.

techniques.comment: SSH brute force against dc-01 — rules 100010 (wrong password) + 100011 (non-existent user) in local_rules.xml, if_matched_sid/frequency/same_source_ip. Verified true positive live (not just wazuh-logtest); firewall-drop active response confirmed firing. Known gap: per-type thresholds, so mixing failure types across both rules evades detection (documented in detection-catalog.md).

SYSVOL FIM escalation on dc-01 — rule 100020, scopes stock FIM rules 550/553/554 (modified/deleted/added) to /var/lib/samba/sysvol via the syscheck 'file' field, escalated to level 12. Verified true positive for add, modify (with full hash diff), and delete. No active response by design (alert-only; auto-reverting a file is riskier than blocking an IP). Untested gap: only exercised via local root on dc-01, not the more realistic remote-SMB write path (needs a second domain host).

Kerberoasting against 3 intentionally-planted Kerberoastable service accounts (svc-sql/svc-backup/svc-web, weak passwords + SPNs, see phase-2-identity/known-weaknesses.md). Enabled Samba's structured auth_json_audit logging (off by default) to get per-TGS-REQ telemetry (Samba's equivalent of Windows Event ID 4769). Rules 100030 (base capture) + 100031 (if_matched_sid + same_field correlation on account, 3+ tickets/60s = level 12). Verified true positive live, AND verified the evasion: a single targeted ticket request produces zero new alerts, confirmed by alert count before/after, not just reasoned about.

Kerberos pre-auth brute force against dc-01 — genuinely different detection surface from the sshd T1110 rules (same telemetry pipeline as Kerberoasting, eventId 4625 = real Windows Event ID). Rules 100040 (base) + 100041 (same_field correlation, 4+/60s). Paired with a real CUSTOM active-response script (disable-ad-account.py, since the stock disable-account command doesn't understand Samba AD accounts) that calls samba-tool to disable/re-enable the targeted account. Verified end-to-end: alert fired -> account's userAccountControl flipped 512->514 -> kinit with the CORRECT password failed with 'credentials have been revoked' -> automatic re-enable at the AR timeout confirmed too. Hard-excludes administrator/krbtgt/guest from automated action to prevent the response itself becoming a DoS vector.

Cron persistence on dc-01 — rule 100050, extends the FIM-escalation pattern proven on SYSVOL to /etc/cron.d, cron.{daily,hourly,weekly,monthly}, and /etc/crontab. Verified true positive by planting a disguised beacon cron job.

Local account creation on dc-01 (the simplest, protocol-independent backdoor once an attacker has root, regardless of how they got it) — rule 100051, FIM on /etc/passwd + /etc/shadow + /etc/sudoers. Also tagged T1098 since the same rule can't distinguish account creation from modifying an existing account's credentials -- verified test specifically exercised useradd (creation), correctly fired on both passwd and shadow writes.

Arguably the highest-value rule in this catalog -- detects an attempt to disable the Wazuh agent, auditd, or samba-ad-dc itself, since every other rule here assumes the monitoring stays alive. Rule 100060, level 13 (highest in the catalog on purpose), pure escalation on the stock sudo rule (5402) with no new telemetry needed. Verified true positive via 'systemctl disable wazuh-agent' -- deliberately not 'stop', which would have killed the agent before it could report the alert about being killed. Documented real evasion: only catches the systemctl/service path, not SIGKILL or firewall-blocking the agent's outbound port; a real deployment needs manager-side disconnection monitoring as the actual backstop.

Encoded/obfuscated PowerShell on ws-01 -- stock rule 92057 (parentImage=powershell.exe + commandLine matches an encoded-command flag alternation). Verified true positive via a parent PowerShell spawning a child with a base64 -EncodedCommand. Part of the Windows/Sysmon batch (techniques 8-12) which is deliberately mostly verification of Wazuh's mature stock Sysmon ruleset rather than new custom rules -- a real, different kind of detection-engineering work than the Linux/AD side.

Registry Run key persistence on ws-01 -- a real gap found in Wazuh's stock Sysmon ruleset and closed. Writing the identical key via reg.exe correctly fired stock rule 92302; the same key via PowerShell's New-ItemProperty (arguably the more realistic real-world method) produced zero alerts, confirmed by direct comparison. Wrote rule 100070 to escalate the base classification rule (92300, level 0, previously silent) generically regardless of which tool performed the write. Verified true positive closing exactly the identified gap. Honest tradeoff named explicitly: broader coverage means firing on legitimate installers too.

Scheduled Task persistence on ws-01, the Windows equivalent of the cron technique on dc-01 -- stock rule 92154 (taskschd.dll module load). Verified true positive via schtasks /create with an onlogon trigger running as SYSTEM.

Windows Event Log clearing on ws-01, the Windows-side counterpart to T1562.001 on the Linux side -- stock rules for Event ID 104 (any log, rule 63104) and Event ID 1102 (Security log specifically, rule 63103, the higher-value anti-forensics target). Verified true positive for both Clear-EventLog and wevtutil cl Security, both alerts carrying real forensic detail (account, domain, client process ID). One of the highest-confidence, lowest-FP rules in the whole catalog.

The most technically involved investigation in this catalog. Stock rule 92900 confirmed correct by code inspection (targetImage=lsass.exe + grantedAccess=0x1010/0x40 + excludes common legitimate callers). Live-fire genuinely attempted, not skipped: Windows Defender blocked the standard comsvcs.dll technique in real time; Tamper Protection silently blocked scripted attempts to disable Defender (GUI-only by design); even with both off, ACCESS_DENIED persisted through elevated admin + SeDebugPrivilege attempts; root cause confirmed via registry -- RunAsPPL=2, LSASS running as Protected Process Light at the strongest tier, Microsoft's real modern mitigation, correctly enabled. wazuh-logtest verification also attempted and found to have a deeper, distinct limitation than the earlier-documented one: it decodes pasted JSON via the generic 'json' decoder, never 'windows_eventchannel', which the rule's full if_sid chain (92900->61612->61600->60004->60000) specifically requires at the base. Defeating PPL for real needs a vulnerable-driver loader -- genuine exploit development, deliberately not attempted even in this authorized isolated lab. Arguably a better portfolio entry than a clean true positive: demonstrates defense-in-depth at three independent layers plus the judgment to know where verification ends and exploit development begins.

INVESTIGATED, NOT ACHIEVED — a real platform limitation, not a skipped step. Tried detecting Domain Admins group-membership changes via every plausible Samba dsdb audit-log facility (dsdb_audit, dsdb_json_audit, dsdb_group_audit, dsdb_group_json_audit, all combinations). Verified the underlying LDAP modification genuinely succeeded each time (samba-tool group listmembers confirmed) and verified the AUTHENTICATION half of the same operation WAS captured correctly by auth_json_audit -- proving the pipeline works and the gap is specific to directory-modification auditing in this Samba build (4.23.6), not a config mistake. A genuine, documented cost of the Samba-vs-Windows-Server DC pivot (docs/design-decisions.md) that the protocol-level equivalence argument doesn't cover. See detection-catalog.md for full methodology.
